title: Failed Head and Shoulders / Rounded Top
teaches: The failed head-and-shoulders as we trade it, the long: a leader above its 200-day draws the top everyone sees, the neckline breaks and the fall stays shallow and is bought back (or the break never comes), the buy is the first trade over the right-shoulder high at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under the trigger day's low while the undercut low is only the invalidation line, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a whipsaw loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: A strong rally, climaxing a more or less extensive advance, on which trading volume becomes very heavy
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: the left shoulder comes at the climax of an extensive advance.

facts.quote: A third rally, but this time on decidedly less volume than accompanied the formation of either the left shoulder or the head, which fails to reach the height of the head
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: the right shoulder is a third rally that fails to reach the head's height.

facts.quote: Until the neckline is broken, a certain percentage of Head-and-Shoulders developments, perhaps 20%, are "saved"
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: perhaps 20% of tops are saved before the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: A Head-and-Shoulders Formation that does not work is a warning that even though there is still some life in the situation, a genuine turn is near.
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: a failed top is a warning that a real turn is near.

facts.quote: It pictures simply and plainly a gradual, progressive, and fairly symmetrical change in the trend direction, produced by a gradual shift in the balance of power between buying and selling.
facts.claim: Edwards and Magee: a rounding turn is a gradual, symmetrical change of trend.

facts.quote: Until that downside violation takes place, however, there is always the pos¬ sibility that the pattern is not really a head and shoulders top and that the uptrend may resume at some point.
facts.claim: Murphy: until the neckline breaks, the uptrend may simply resume.

facts.quote: This might be sufficient cause to liquidate long positions, but not necessarily enough to justify new short sales.
facts.claim: Murphy: the topping signs justify selling longs, not new shorts.

facts.quote: At a top, once the neckline has been broken on the down¬ side, any decisive close back above the neckline is a serious warn¬ ing that the initial breakdown was probably a bad signal
facts.claim: Murphy: a decisive close back over the neckline says the breakdown was a bad signal.

facts.quote: probably the best known and most reliable of all major reversal patterns
facts.claim: Murphy: the head and shoulders is the best known reversal pattern.

facts.quote: Without a prior uptrend to reverse, there cannot be a Head and Shoulders reversal pattern (or any reversal pattern, for that matter).
facts.claim: StockCharts: no prior uptrend, no head and shoulders top.

facts.quote: The head and shoulders pattern isn't complete, and the uptrend is not reversed until the neckline support is broken.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the top is not complete until the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: Sometimes, but certainly not always, the price will return to the support break and offer a second chance to sell.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the return move to the broken neckline is a second chance to sell.

facts.quote: While symmetry is preferred, sometimes the shoulders can be out of whack.
facts.claim: StockCharts: symmetry is preferred, not required.

facts.quote: A three-peak pattern with the middle peak above the others.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: three peaks, the middle one highest.

facts.quote: The two shoulders should peak near the same price, be nearly the same distance from the head, and look similar
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the two shoulders should peak near the same price.

facts.quote: Wait for confirmation before placing a trade.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: wait for confirmation before trading the top.

facts.quote: breaks out downward and drops no more than 10%, turns around, and then closes above the top of the head-and-shoulders
facts.claim: Bulkowski's busted top: a break that drops no more than 10% and turns around.

facts.quote: To trade this busted chart pattern, place a buy order a penny above the head (the highest high in the chart pattern).
facts.claim: Bulkowski buys the busted top a penny above the head.

facts.quote: 30% of them will triple bust
facts.claim: Bulkowski: 30% of busted tops triple bust, so failures whipsaw.

facts.quote: A busted pattern occurs when price breaks out in one direction and moves less than 10% away from the breakout price
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a bust moves less than 10% from the breakout price before reversing.

facts.quote: Prices form a gentle curve, a half moon shape.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a rounding top is a gentle half-moon curve.

facts.quote: A close above the highest high signals an upward breakout. Downward breakouts are a close below the lower of the two rims (the lowest low in the pattern).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a rounding top breaks up over its highest high and down under the lower rim.

facts.quote: Heavy breakout volume suggests better performance.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: heavy breakout volume suggests better performance.

facts.quote: Tall patterns perform better than short ones.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: tall patterns perform better than short ones.

facts.quote: The advance today, May 18, penetrated the May 10 right shoulder high and officially completed the failure pattern.
facts.claim: Brandt: the failure pattern completes when price penetrates the right-shoulder high.

facts.quote: The market should probably not take out Wednesday's low (652-3/4).
facts.claim: Brandt's line in the sand was the trigger day's low.

facts.quote: I consider H&S failure patterns to be very tradable chart developments.
facts.claim: Brandt: H&S failures are very tradable.

facts.quote: The target of 733 is based on projecting the distance between the April 26 high and the May 12 low (which is 69 cents) upward from the right shoulder high of 664.
facts.claim: Brandt's target: the head-to-post-break-low distance added to the right-shoulder high.

facts.quote: Unfortunately novice market analysts are way to quick to mislabel market action as a H&S configuration.
facts.claim: Brandt: novices mislabel ordinary action as a head and shoulders.

facts.quote: It is not unusual for H&S tops to be brief, whereas H&S bottom patterns tend to be much longer in duration.
facts.claim: Brandt: tops are often brief.

facts.quote: Remember the only way to trade a H&S pattern is to trade the failure of it.
facts.claim: Bracco: the only way to trade a head and shoulders is to trade its failure.

facts.quote: this is why coming out of corrections I try to get a position in TQQQ and SOXL.
facts.claim: Bracco uses the failed top coming out of corrections.

facts.quote: the best way to trade a head and shoulders top is to buy the failed breakdown of it.
facts.claim: Bracco: buy the failed breakdown of a head and shoulders top.

facts.quote: Turning $333 head and shoulder neckline into support is step 1. Step 2 is remounting the 50SMA and the 20EMA.
facts.claim: Bracco: neckline to support first, then remount the 50-day.

facts.quote: Failed Head and Shoulders breakdown at $325. 50SMA the line in the sand to stay above.
facts.claim: Bracco: the 50-day is the line in the sand on a failed breakdown.

facts.quote: Stop at LOD if this triggers. My stops are always LOD until I can raise them to breakeven
facts.claim: Our stop habit: the low of the day until it can go to breakeven.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; if it does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit and only moves up.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: past 2R in the first 30 minutes, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day; shorts only below it.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day or the 21-day; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

facts.quote: In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
facts.claim: D46: in a Red market, mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day.

facts.quote: The house meaning is the long: the breakdown everyone sees never comes, or comes and fails, and the squeeze fuels the next leg up.
facts.claim: We trade the failed top long: the squeeze fuels the next leg up.

facts.quote: The first trade above the right-shoulder high (the dome high for a rounded top) after the failure.
facts.claim: The trigger: the first trade over the right-shoulder high after the failure.

facts.quote: A few cents under the trigger day's low, with a real stop order.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the trigger day's low.

facts.quote: The low of the failed breakdown is the invalidation line, not the stop.
facts.claim: The undercut low is the invalidation line, not the stop.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: a fall of more than 10% under the neckline. The top worked; this setup is gone.
facts.claim: A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked; no setup.

facts.quote: Version A (allowed, graded lower): no close under the neckline; price turns up from the right shoulder.
facts.claim: Version A: no close under the neckline; price turns up from the right shoulder; the lesser form.

facts.quote: A brief, shallow undercut (under 6% below the neckline) is the A+ form; 6% to 10% grades lower.
facts.claim: A shallow undercut under 6% is the A+ form; 6% to 10% grades lower.

facts.quote: No hard volume rule. Trigger-day volume 1.25x or more of the 50-day average is a grading plus.
facts.claim: Volume is a grade cue: 1.25x the 50-day average is a plus, never a gate.

facts.quote: The close is above the 50-day SMA on the trigger day.
facts.claim: On the trigger day the close is above the 50-day.

facts.quote: An uptrend into the pattern: the close is above a rising 200-day SMA when the left shoulder forms, and the head is at least 25% above the lowest low of the 6 months before the left shoulder.
facts.claim: Prior trend: above a rising 200-day at the left shoulder; the head at least 25% over the prior six months' low.

facts.quote: For version B the trigger comes within 40 bars of the failure; the failure itself within 60 bars of the right shoulder.
facts.claim: The trigger comes within 40 sessions of the failure; the failure within 60 of the right shoulder.

facts.quote: After the buy: a close back under the neckline is a failure of the failure; the stop should already be above that.
facts.claim: After the buy, a close back under the neckline is the failure of the failure.

facts.quote: A reference, not a rule: the head is the first place sellers may return; Brandt's target is the right-shoulder high plus the distance from the head down to the post-break low.
facts.claim: The head is a reference where sellers may return, not an exit rule.

facts.quote: Grade it lower when the stock has already run for a year or more: a failed top late in a long advance can be the last push.
facts.claim: A failed top late in a long advance grades lower; it can be the last push.

facts.quote: A cue: best when the market itself is correcting or just turning up and the stock's top fails anyway, the leader refusing to break while the market falls.
facts.claim: Best when the market is correcting and the leader refuses to break.

facts.quote: Never short the right shoulder before the neckline breaks, and the neckline break is not taught as a short setup
facts.claim: We never short the right shoulder before the break; the break is not a short setup here.

facts.quote: its neckline is the lower rim (the lowest low of the arc); the trigger is the dome high.
facts.claim: A rounded top's neckline is the lower rim; its trigger is the dome high.

facts.quote: A flat base holds one range 15% deep or less with a flat top tapped twice and breaks out over it; a rounded top is a dome that first broke its lower rim (or sagged toward it) and then recovered
facts.claim: A flat base is a box broken upward; a rounded top failure is a dome that lost its rim and recovered.

facts.quote: A 2B breaks one prior swing low and is bought the moment price reclaims that low, within 1 to 3 sessions, with the stop under the new low.
facts.claim: A 2B is one broken low bought on the reclaim within 1 to 3 sessions.

facts.quote: A failed H&S has three peaks over a neckline and waits for the trade over the right-shoulder high, with the stop under that day's low.
facts.claim: A failed H&S has three peaks over a neckline and waits for the right-shoulder high.

facts.quote: A mean-reversion long buys the turn on the flush day itself, into a level, and is out in 1 to 5 sessions at the average
facts.claim: A mean-reversion long buys the flush day and is out in 1 to 5 sessions.

facts.quote: Buying the first bounce back to the neckline. That is the return move the short sellers expect; wait for the right-shoulder high.
facts.claim: A named mistake: buying the first bounce back to the neckline.

facts.quote: Using the undercut low as the stop. It is usually far more than 3% away.
facts.claim: A named mistake: the undercut low as the stop.

facts.quote: Calling every three bumps a head-and-shoulders.
facts.claim: A named mistake: calling every three bumps a head and shoulders.

facts.quote: Best when the market itself is correcting and the stock refuses to break down.
facts.claim: Best when the market is correcting and the stock refuses to break down.

facts.quote: The breakdown either never comes (A) or comes, falls under 10%, and is bought back (B).
facts.claim: Version A: the break never comes. Version B: it comes, falls under 10%, and is bought back.

facts.quote: Count the tries: at most 3 in a week and 6 in a month. Failures whipsaw; a second entry over the same level is allowed.
facts.claim: Failures whipsaw; a second entry over the same level is allowed, at most 3 tries a week.

facts.quote: If the stop is more than about 3% under the entry, size it down to the risk or skip.
facts.claim: A stop wider than about 3%: size down to the risk or skip.

facts.quote: A Green or Yellow reading (F65); in Orange, A+ only.
facts.claim: Green or Yellow; in Orange, A+ only.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: a close under the 200-day.
facts.claim: A close under the 200-day before the trigger ends the setup.

facts.quote: The failure fails: price closes back under the neckline and the top works after all (Bulkowski's double bust), or the trigger whipsaws through a tight day-low stop before the real move (AAPL 2026).
facts.claim: The failure mode: the failure fails, or the trigger whipsaws through the day-low stop before the real move.

facts.quote: The close is above the 200-day SMA on the trigger day (hard).
facts.claim: The close is above the 200-day on the trigger day, a hard rule.

facts.quote: A market order once price is through the level, during regular hours.
facts.claim: A market order once price is through the level, in regular hours.

facts.quote: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.
facts.claim: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.

facts.quote: A real stop order with the broker. It only moves up.
facts.claim: A real stop order with the broker; it only moves up.

facts.quote: Chasing a gap far over the right shoulder (LULU 2023, 11.4%).
facts.claim: A named mistake: chasing a gap far over the right shoulder.

facts.quote: Stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
facts.claim: Breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.

facts.quote: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out if that is past 2R.
facts.claim: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out past 2R.

facts.quote: Time stop: still under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.
facts.claim: Under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.

facts.quote: Trail the last third: a close under the 10-day for a fast mover, under the 21-day for a steadier one.
facts.claim: Trail the last third on the 10-day or the 21-day.

facts.quote: The position is at most 1% of average daily volume.
facts.claim: The position is at most 1% of average daily volume.

facts.quote: Price $10 or more and $20 million or more traded a day on average.
facts.claim: Price $10 or more and $20 million a day or more.

facts.quote: a failed H&S waits weeks for the undercut to be bought back and then for the trade over the right-shoulder high, and holds for a trend.
facts.claim: A failed H&S waits weeks for the undercut to be bought back, then holds for a trend.

facts.quote: Version B (preferred): at least one close under the neckline, or an intraday undercut of the right armpit low, that does not fall more than 10% under the neckline before the trigger.
facts.claim: Version B: a close under the neckline, or an undercut of the right armpit low, bought back before falling 10%.

facts.quote: At entry, no more than 10% above the 10-day average.
facts.claim: At entry, no more than 10% above the 10-day average.

facts.quote: Forgetting Edwards and Magee's warning: a failed top late in a long advance can be the last push (GOOGL 2026).
facts.claim: A named mistake: forgetting that a late failed top can be the last push.

facts.quote: Sell a third at 3R.
facts.claim: Sell a third at 3R.

facts.quote: Sell a third at 5R.
facts.claim: Sell a third at 5R.

facts.quote: If it opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.
FDX, trigger 2003-03-19: head 47.22, neckline 40.82, 13.6% tall; buy 42.98, stop 42.42 (1.3%); 17.3R, 3R in 1 day.

facts.quote: A clean three-peak top at the 2003 bear-market bottom; the break under the neckline failed in two weeks, the trigger day was the earnings reaction day (report before the open, 2.5x volume), and price never looked back.
facts.claim: FDX: a clean top at the 2003 bottom; the break failed in two weeks; the trigger was the earnings reaction day.
MGM, trigger 2004-09-14: shoulders 22.77 and 22.70, head 24.89, neckline 21.22; 6.1% under; buy 22.71, stop 22.30; 23.7R, 3R in 5 days.

facts.quote: Shoulders within 0.3% of each other, a flat neckline, a four-week failed breakdown, then a trigger over the right shoulder with 1.9x volume. The most symmetrical pattern of the ten.
facts.claim: MGM: shoulders within 0.3%, a flat neckline, a four-week failed breakdown, a trigger on 1.9x volume.
SPG, trigger 2005-11-11: head 12.4% over the neckline 65.03; 7.1% under, low 61.03; buy 69.53, stop 68.76 (1.1%); 11.9R, 3R in 6 days.

facts.quote: the trigger came with the stock back over the 50-day. Shows that the invalidation line (61) was far from a usable stop; the trigger day's low gave 1.1%.
facts.claim: SPG: a seven-week break recovered; the trigger came back over the 50-day; the invalidation line at 61 was far from a usable stop.
BXP, trigger 2010-02-26: neckline 63.38, low 61.50, 3.0% under; buy 68.02, stop 67.20; 18.8R.

facts.quote: Nearly level shoulders (0.4% apart), a flat neckline, a two-week undercut, then a trigger that held above the 50-day. A learner can draw every line on this one.
facts.claim: BXP: level shoulders, a flat neckline, a two-week undercut, a trigger above the 50-day.
MCO, trigger 2011-01-06: right shoulder 27.71; a 1.0% undercut; buy 27.98, stop 27.66; 21.1R, 3R in 1 day.

facts.quote: The trigger day gapped 1% over the level (entry at the open, inside the 4% chase limit) on 2.6x volume
facts.claim: MCO: the trigger day gapped 1% over the level, bought at the open inside the chase limit, on 2.6x volume.

facts.quote: The shallow version: the head only 9% over the neckline and a one-day, 1% undercut. Teaches that the failure can be small.
facts.claim: MCO: a shallow top and a one-day 1% undercut; the failure can be small.

facts.quote: A slow one: the trigger came on average volume (1.0x) and 3R took three weeks, then the stock ran 25%. Shows the trade does not need a volume spike to work, and why the trail (10-day or 21-day) matters.
facts.claim: ICLR: triggered on 1.0x volume, 3R took three weeks, then a 25% run; no volume spike needed.
MUSA, trigger 2022-03-15: head 202.20, right shoulder 184.96, neckline 176.18; 6.8% under; buy 184.97, stop 182.98; 39.0R, 3R in 1 day.

facts.quote: The best outcome of the ten: a 7% break under the neckline during the early-2022 correction, recovered in three weeks; the trigger over the right shoulder was followed by a 40% run.
facts.claim: MUSA: a 7% break during the early-2022 correction, recovered in three weeks, then a 40% run.

facts.quote: Equal shoulders (0.8% apart), a flat neckline, a seven-week failed breakdown to 109, then a trigger on 1.3x volume above the 50-day.
facts.claim: TOL: equal shoulders, a flat neckline, a seven-week failed breakdown, a trigger on 1.3x volume above the 50-day.
NFLX, trigger 2025-04-21: buy 99.88, stop 97.26 (2.6%); 13.1R, 3R in 3 days.

facts.quote: The trigger day was the earnings reaction day (report 2025-04-17 after the close; 2.0x volume); the open was under the level, so the entry was at the level, not a chase.
facts.claim: NFLX: the trigger was the earnings reaction day, after the report; the entry was at the level.

facts.claim: DDOG, trigger 2025-01-28: buy 147.65, stop 143.35; stopped on day 1 at a low of 141.96.

facts.quote: 0R, then the stock lost 44.7% within 60 sessions.
facts.claim: DDOG: 0R, then a 44.7% loss within 60 sessions; the top worked.
GILD, trigger 2014-12-19: buy 107.59, stop 104.59; the next open was 96.73, a gap under the stop.

facts.quote: The fill was far under the stop; the stock lost 20.1% within 60 sessions: the top worked.
facts.claim: GILD: the top worked; the stock lost 20.1% within 60 sessions.

questions.q: Which way do we trade a head-and-shoulders top?
choices: Long, when the breakdown fails
Short, when the neckline breaks
Short, as the right shoulder forms
Long, when the neckline breaks
questions.why: Long, when the breakdown fails. The breakdown everyone sees never comes, or comes and fails, and the squeeze fuels the next leg up. Bracco: the only way to trade a head and shoulders is to trade its failure. We never short the right shoulder before the neckline breaks, and a break is not taught here as a short setup. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked, and the setup is gone.
questions.lesson_line: The top everyone sees is the trade when it fails. We buy the failure.

wrong.Short, when the neckline breaks: The break is not taught here as a short setup. Of breaks from tops that formed above the 200-day, 70% stayed above it, where we never short.
wrong.Short, as the right shoulder forms: We never short the right shoulder before the neckline breaks. Nothing has failed yet.
wrong.Long, when the neckline breaks: Nothing has failed at the break. The buy waits for the failure, over the right-shoulder high.

questions.simple: We buy, not short, once a breakdown fails, because the squeeze after the failure fuels the next leg up.

deeper.example: FDX, March 2003: a clean three-peak top at the 2003 bear-market bottom. The break failed in two weeks. We bought 42.98 with the stop at 42.42, 1.3% away. It reached 3R in 1 day and 17.3R at best.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-001, the direction)
fixed before

questions.q: The neckline broke, the fall stayed shallow, and price came back. By Brandt, the failure is complete when?
choices: A trade over the right-shoulder high
A first bounce back to the neckline
A touch of the undercut low
A first close back over the 50-day line
questions.answer: A trade over the right-shoulder high
questions.why: Over the right-shoulder high. Brandt: the advance penetrated the right-shoulder high and officially completed the failure pattern. Our trigger is the same level: the first trade over it after the failure. A bounce back to the neckline is the return move the short sellers expect, not the signal.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the right-shoulder high. The failure is complete when price trades through it, not on the bounce below it.

wrong.A first bounce back to the neckline: Buying the first bounce back to the neckline is a named mistake. That is the return move the short sellers expect.
wrong.A touch of the undercut low: The undercut low is the invalidation line, not the signal. Brandt completes the failure over the right-shoulder high, well above it.
wrong.A first close back over the 50-day line: The 50-day is a check on the trigger day, not the completion. Brandt completes the failure over the right-shoulder high.

questions.simple: The failure is complete when price trades over the right-shoulder high, not on a bounce back to the neckline.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the trigger)
fixed before

questions.q: The stop on a failed head-and-shoulders goes a few cents under the trigger day's low.
questions.why: True. The stop goes a few cents under the trigger day's low, with a real stop order. Our stop habit: the low of the day, until it can go to breakeven. Stop first: the size comes from the stop, and if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. The undercut low is only the invalidation line, not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the trigger day's low.
questions.simple: True, the stop sits a few cents under the trigger day's low, not exactly on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: We may buy a failed head-and-shoulders when the trigger day's close is under the 200-day.
questions.why: False. The close must be above the 200-day on the trigger day. That is a hard rule. The rulebook bars longs below the 200-day simple moving average.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there is no failed top to buy.
questions.simple: False, because we do not buy a long when the close is under the 200-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A head-and-shoulders top has three peaks with the ___ one highest.
questions.why: The middle one. A head-and-shoulders top is a three-peak pattern with the middle peak above the others (Bulkowski). The third rally, the right shoulder, fails to reach the height of the head (Edwards and Magee). Symmetry is preferred, not required.
questions.lesson_line: Three peaks, the head in the middle, the shoulders lower on each side.
questions.simple: The middle peak is the highest, which makes it the head, and the two shoulders sit lower.

reasons: two agreeing Tier 2 sources, a stable definition

questions.q: What is the low of the failed breakdown used for?
choices: The setup's invalidation line
The stop, a few cents under it
The price where we buy back in
The target for the first trim
questions.why: The invalidation line. In our run a stop under the failed-break low sat a median 9.3% away, and only 4% were within 3%. Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy, so that low is too far to be the stop. Using it as the stop is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: The undercut low is the invalidation line. The trigger day's low is the stop.

wrong.The stop, a few cents under it: Using the undercut low as the stop is a named mistake. It is usually far more than 3% away.
wrong.The price where we buy back in: The buy is over the right-shoulder high, well above that low.
wrong.The target for the first trim: The first trim is a third at 3R, a multiple of the risk. It is not a price taken from that low.

questions.simple: That low is the invalidation line, and it sits too far from the buy to work as a stop.

deeper.example: SPG, November 2005: the break ran seven weeks down to a low of 61.03. The buy was 69.53, and the trigger day's low gave a stop of 68.76, 1.1% away. A stop at 61.03 would have been far from usable.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (the invalidation line)

questions.q: Version B means the neckline broke, the fall stayed small, and price was bought back.
questions.why: True. Version B is a real break that fails: the neckline breaks, the fall stays under 10%, and the break is bought back. Bulkowski calls it a busted top: it drops no more than 10%, turns around, and closes above the top of the pattern. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked.
questions.lesson_line: A real break that fails is version B, the form we want.
questions.simple: True, because a break that drops under 10% and is bought back is the failed breakdown we want.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-109, versions A and B)

questions.q: The right shoulder is forming and the neckline is still intact. Our move?
choices: No short; wait and watch
Short the right shoulder
Buy the right shoulder
Wait, then buy the neckline break
questions.why: No short. Murphy: the topping signs might be cause to liquidate long positions, but not necessarily enough to justify new short sales. Until the neckline breaks, the uptrend may simply resume, and StockCharts says the pattern is not complete. We never short the right shoulder before the break, and we do not teach the break as a short setup.
questions.lesson_line: A top that has not broken is a picture, not a trade.

wrong.Short the right shoulder: We never short the right shoulder before the neckline breaks. Nothing has broken; the uptrend may resume.
wrong.Buy the right shoulder: No trigger yet. The buy comes over the right-shoulder high after a failure.
wrong.Wait, then buy the neckline break: Nothing has failed at the break. The buy waits for the failure, over the right-shoulder high.

questions.simple: Do not short. The top is not complete until the neckline breaks, and the uptrend may simply resume.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-001, no short)

questions.q: A head-and-shoulders top needs an uptrend in front of it.
questions.why: True. A head-and-shoulders top is a reversal pattern, so it needs an advance to reverse. StockCharts: without a prior uptrend to reverse, there cannot be a head and shoulders reversal pattern. Edwards and Magee open the pattern with a strong rally that climaxes an extensive advance. Our card makes it measurable: the close is above a rising 200-day when the left shoulder forms, and the head is at least 25% above the lowest low of the 6 months before it. Three bumps with no run in front are not a top.
questions.lesson_line: No advance, no top to fail. Check the run before the shape.
questions.simple: True, because a top reverses an uptrend, so with no uptrend in front there is nothing for it to reverse.

reasons: two agreeing Tier 2 sources, a stable idea
the 25% test is our card's own number

questions.q: At 10:40 the stock trades through the right-shoulder high. How do you buy?
choices: Market order, now
Limit at the neckline
Wait for the close
Premarket tomorrow
questions.why: Market order, now. Entries are market orders, sent once price is through the level and only in regular trading hours. At 10:40 it is regular hours. No new buys outside regular trading hours, so premarket tomorrow is out too. A limit at the neckline sits far under price and does not buy the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Through the level, in hours, at market. No debate at the fill.

wrong.Limit at the neckline: A limit at the neckline sits under price and never fills on the trigger. The neckline is behind us.
wrong.Wait for the close: The trigger is the first trade over the level, not the close.
wrong.Premarket tomorrow: No new buys outside regular trading hours.

questions.simple: Buy at market now, because the price is through the level and it is regular hours.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After a failed breakdown, Bracco's line in the sand to stay above is the ___-day.
questions.why: 50. Bracco on the SMH failed breakdown: 50SMA the line in the sand to stay above. He calls turning the neckline into support step 1 and remounting the 50-day step 2. Our card asks for the trigger-day close above the 50-day. The 200-day is a separate and harder test: the trigger-day close must also be above it. Bracco's line here is the 50.
questions.lesson_line: Neckline to support first, then back over the 50-day. Then the trigger.
questions.simple: The answer is 50, because Bracco treats the 50-day line as the one to stay above after a failed breakdown.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion and Bracco's published posts

questions.q: A failed head-and-shoulders may be bought two sessions before the company reports.
questions.why: False. The rulebook bars new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. Our card says the same: no new buy in the 3 sessions before one. Two sessions out is inside that window. A trade already open may hold through a report only if it is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before earnings. Wait for the report to pass.
questions.simple: False, because new buys are barred in the 3 days before a report, and two sessions is inside that.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.story: A leader draws a three-peak top and the right shoulder sits in place. Every close stays above the neckline. Price turns up from the right shoulder and trades over its high.
questions.q: Which version is this?
choices: Version A, no break came
Version B, a failed breakdown
Not a failed top at all
A 2B, a broken low bought back
questions.why: Version A. There is no close under the neckline, and price turns up from the right shoulder. Edwards and Magee: until the neckline is broken, perhaps 20% of these tops are saved. By our current default, version A is allowed but graded lower than B, a real break bought back.
questions.lesson_line: No break, then a turn up: version A. A break bought back: version B, the one we want.

wrong.Version B, a failed breakdown: B needs a real close under the neckline that is then bought back. Here there was no break.
wrong.Not a failed top at all: The pattern was saved before the break. That counts, as the lesser version.
wrong.A 2B, a broken low bought back: A 2B breaks one prior swing low and is bought when price reclaims it. Here nothing broke, and the setup has three peaks over a neckline.

questions.simple: This is version A, because no close came under the neckline and price turned up from the right shoulder.

deeper.counter: Version A is the common one in our data: 32,514 long-A triggers averaged +0.04R, against 6,543 for version B at +0.11R. Version A is real but thinner.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-109, versions A and B)
fixed before

questions.q: A slow dome with no single peak standing out. What is its neckline?
choices: The lower rim, the arc's low
The dome high, the top of the arc
The 50-day moving average
A line across the two high points
questions.answer: The lower rim, the arc's low
questions.why: The lower rim, the lowest low of the arc. A rounded top is a gentle half-moon curve. Bulkowski: a downward breakout is a close below the lower of the two rims, the lowest low in the pattern. The dome high is the top of the arc, not the floor.
questions.lesson_line: A dome has no shoulders. Its floor is the lower rim.

wrong.The dome high, the top of the arc: The dome high is the top of the arc. The neckline is the floor.
wrong.The 50-day moving average: A moving average is context, not the pattern's floor.
wrong.A line across the two high points: A dome has no two peaks to join. The floor is the lowest low of the arc.

questions.simple: The neckline of a dome is its lower rim, the lowest low of the arc.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-002, the rounded top)
fixed before

questions.q: The stop on this trade may stay in your head as long as you act on it.
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False, because the stop must be a real order with the broker, not a plan in your head.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, A4)

questions.q: On a version B setup, what is the longest the trigger may wait after the failure?
choices: 40 sessions
10 sessions
60 sessions
100 sessions
questions.why: 40 sessions. Our card's window for version B: the trigger comes within 40 sessions of the failure, and the failure itself within 60 sessions of the right shoulder. It is a card rule for this setup, not a law of the market.
questions.lesson_line: Version B has a clock. The trigger comes within 40 sessions of the failure.

wrong.10 sessions: Too tight. The card gives the trigger up to 40 sessions after the failure.
wrong.60 sessions: That is the other window: the failure itself comes within 60 sessions of the right shoulder. The trigger gets 40.
wrong.100 sessions: Too long. The card's window is 40 sessions.

questions.simple: Our card gives the trigger up to 40 sessions after the failure.

reasons: the 40 and 60 session windows are our card's proposed rule

questions.q: Head 47.22, neckline 40.82. How tall is the pattern, head to neckline, as a percent of the head?
questions.why: 13.6%. Head minus neckline, divided by the head: 47.22 minus 40.82, divided by 47.22, rounded to one decimal. That is the height of FDX's 2003 top. StockCharts measures a top's height from the neckline to the top of the head.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the top from the head to the neckline, as a percent of the head.
questions.simple: The pattern is 13.6% tall: take the head minus the neckline, then divide by the head.

reasons: a computed key
fixed before

questions.story: The neckline broke three weeks ago. The stock is now 14% under it and still sliding.
questions.q: Still a failed head-and-shoulders candidate?
choices: No; past 10% the top worked
Yes, once back over the neckline
Yes; buy the next bounce
No; any close below it kills it
questions.why: No. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked, and this setup is gone. Bulkowski defines a bust as a break that moves less than 10% from the breakout price before it turns, and this one is 14% under. A failed head-and-shoulders is a shallow break that is bought back, not a deep slide. One close under the neckline is allowed in version B; a fall past 10% is not.
questions.lesson_line: A failure is a shallow break. A deep one is a top that worked.

wrong.Yes; buy the next bounce: At 14% under there is no setup to buy. And buying the first bounce back to the neckline is a named mistake on our card.
wrong.Yes, once back over the neckline: The setup is gone once the fall passes 10% under the neckline. A climb back later does not bring it back.
wrong.No; any close below it kills it: Version B needs at least one close under the neckline. A close under it does not end the setup; a fall past 10% does.

questions.simple: No. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked, so the setup is gone.

reasons: the deep-break line is our card's proposed rule

questions.q: The first trim on a failed head-and-shoulders winner is a third at 3R.
questions.why: True. The hard rule is a third off at 3R. The rulebook says ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R for the first trim, and the levels are adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: The hard rule: the first third comes off at 3R.
questions.simple: True, because the hard rule is to sell a third at 3R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: The reading is Orange. A failed top triggers in a leader, but it grades below A+. May you buy it?
choices: No; Orange allows only A+ setups
No; Orange means cash, no new longs
Yes, at half size, since it is Orange
Yes; a leader's grade does not matter
questions.answer: No; Orange allows only A+ setups
questions.why: No. This one grades below A+. Our market reading is a guide: Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions, Yellow is smaller and fewer, Orange is only A+ setups, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. In Orange this one waits.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the pattern. Orange buys A+ and nothing else.

wrong.No; Orange means cash, no new longs: Red is mostly cash and shorts. Orange still allows A+ setups.
wrong.Yes, at half size, since it is Orange: Orange is about grade. Only A+ setups pass; a lower grade stays on the bench at any size.
wrong.Yes; a leader's grade does not matter: In Orange the grade is the test. Only A+ setups pass, even in a leader.

questions.simple: No. In Orange only A+ setups are allowed, and this one grades lower.

reasons: rests on the owner's market reading, F65

questions.story: A stock undercut one prior swing low on Tuesday and reclaimed it by Thursday. There is no three-peak top above it and no neckline.
questions.q: Which setup is that?
choices: A 2B, bought on the way back
A failed head-and-shoulders long
A rounded top with a slow dome
A flat-base breakout entry
questions.answer: A 2B, bought on the way back
questions.why: A 2B. It breaks one prior swing low and is bought the moment price reclaims that low, within 1 to 3 sessions. The story has one low undercut on Tuesday and taken back by Thursday, with no three-peak top and no neckline. A failed head-and-shoulders has three peaks over a neckline and waits for the trade over the right-shoulder high. A rounded top is a gentle half-moon curve.
questions.lesson_line: Count the peaks and find the trigger. One low reclaimed is a 2B; three peaks and a wait is ours.

wrong.A failed head-and-shoulders long: Three peaks over a neckline are missing. One low broken and taken back is the 2B.
wrong.A rounded top with a slow dome: A rounded top is a gentle half-moon curve. This story is one sharp undercut and a quick reclaim.
wrong.A flat-base breakout entry: A flat base is one tight range with a flat top, broken upward. This stock broke a low and took it back.

questions.simple: A 2B, because one low was broken and quickly taken back, with no three peaks and no neckline.

reasons: rests on the held trigger decision D-003
key reworded so it no longer repeats the story's word

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After a third at 3R, the next third comes off by default at ___R, then the last third trails.
questions.why: 5R. After the first third at 3R, our rulebook takes another third at 5R and trails the last third. The levels are adjustable in the rulebook, and 5R is the default. The first third is a hard rule at 3R; the second is the default, not a law.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R and 5R before the open. The trims are decided, not debated.
questions.simple: The second third comes off at 5R, and the last third rides the trail.

questions.lesson_line: Measure the undercut from the neckline. Shallow and brief is the one you want.
questions.simple: The undercut is 3.0% deep, found by dividing the drop under the neckline by the neckline.

reasons: a computed key
rests on proposed card lines (6% and 10%)

questions.story: The right-shoulder high is 327.76. After earnings the stock opens at 365.00, 11.4% over it, and the failure is complete on the gap.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Skip it; the fill is a chase
Buy the open; the failure is done
Buy half size right at the open
Buy, stop under the neckline
questions.answer: Skip it; the fill is a chase
questions.why: Skip it. Our rule is never to buy more than 4% above the buy point, and this open is 11.4% over the right-shoulder high. On our card a gap past that line means skip, or wait for a retest of the level. Chasing a gap far over the right shoulder is a named mistake: LULU in 2023 was bought at 365.00 after an earnings gap and lost 1.0R. Chasing costs size, not risk, because the stop stays under the buy point.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. A gap far past the level is not my entry.

wrong.Buy the open; the failure is done: The failure is complete, but the open is 11.4% over the level. The stop stays under the buy point, so a fill this far up leaves a wide stop and a small position.
wrong.Buy, stop under the neckline: A stop under the neckline sits far below a fill 11.4% over the level. The stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.
wrong.Buy half size right at the open: Half size still pays the chase price. The rule limits how far above the buy point you may buy, whatever the size.

questions.simple: Skip it, because buying 11.4% above the level is a chase.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule C28 and the held decision D-022
the 'wait for a retest' half comes from our card statement only
the answer has a hedge, skip or wait

questions.story: You bought the trigger over 320.28 and were stopped the next day at 315.40. The neckline still holds. Today it trades back over 320.28.
questions.q: Buy again?
choices: Yes; a new trade with a new stop
No; only one try per pattern
Yes, with a wider stop this time
No; the pattern has already failed
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade with a new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Today's trade back over 320.28 is that new trigger. The stop is set fresh for this trade and is never widened to dodge another whipsaw. Count the tries: at most 3 in a week and 6 in a month. Failures whipsaw, and a second entry over the same level is allowed. In our AAPL example the first try was a whipsaw, and the stock then rose 11% within 60 sessions without the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A whipsaw is not a verdict on the setup. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No; only one try per pattern: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop this time: Every new trade gets its own stop, a few cents under its own trigger day's low. Widening it to dodge another whipsaw breaks the stop-first rule.
wrong.No; the pattern has already failed: The trade failed; the pattern triggered again. A second entry over the same level is allowed.

questions.simple: Yes, as a new trade with its own stop, as long as you are inside the limit of 3 tries a week.

deeper.trap: A whipsaw feels like proof that the setup is wrong. The data say otherwise. AAPL was stopped on day 1, at a low of 312.80, and the stock then rose 11% within 60 sessions without the trade. The stop did its job. The mistake is to skip the next valid trigger, or to buy it with a wider stop, because the last one hurt.

reasons: rests on the owner's rules B21 and E56

questions.q: When does the stop move to breakeven on this trade?
choices: 2R to 5R, at the first trim
At 1R, as soon as it arrives
6R to 10R, after the second trim
On the first close above entry
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. Our rulebook says to move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally, and the card sets it at the first trim. The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R, so 3R is the natural moment. After that the stop only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Move the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.

wrong.At 1R, as soon as it arrives: Too soon. The card puts breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.
wrong.6R to 10R, after the second trim: Too late. The card puts breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally, at the first trim by default.
wrong.On the first close above entry: The rulebook sets breakeven by R, not by a close. A single higher close can come long before 2R.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, and by default at the first trim, which is when a third comes off.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule B19

questions.story: You bought at 107.59, stop 104.59. The next morning the stock opens at 96.73, far under your stop.
questions.q: What is the rule?
choices: First 30-minute low; past 2R, out
Hold; gaps usually fill by the close
Wait for a close back over the stop
Move the stop down to the gap open
questions.why: The first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop, and if that puts the loss past 2R, you get out. Here the open, 96.73, was already past 2R from the 107.59 buy, so out. The top worked: GILD lost 20.1% within 60 sessions. The stop never moves down or wider, except by this one gap rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception, and it has a 2R ceiling.

wrong.Wait for a close back over the stop: The rule has no wait for a reclaim. The first 30 minutes decide, with a ceiling of 2R.
wrong.Move the stop down to the gap open: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception, and it uses the first 30-minute low with a ceiling of 2R, not the open.
wrong.Hold; gaps usually fill by the close: Not our rule. No rule waits for a gap to fill. The first 30 minutes decide, with a ceiling of 2R.

questions.simple: A gap through the stop means the first 30-minute low is the new stop, and past 2R you sell.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
fixed before

questions.q: A failed head-and-shoulders long still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.why: True. Our rulebook has a time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. It applies to this long like any other trade. The count is trading days, and the test is whether the trade has reached 1R.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: True. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold so the money can work elsewhere.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule C33

questions.story: You bought over the right-shoulder high at 147.65 with the stop at 143.35. The next day the low prints 141.96 and the close is back under the neckline.
questions.q: What happened?
choices: The failure failed; the stop fired
A shakeout; buy it back now
Hold; the neckline is support
questions.answer: The failure failed; the stop fired
questions.why: The failure failed. A close back under the neckline after the buy is the failure of the failure, and the stop was already above it. DDOG then lost 44.7% within 60 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: When the failure fails, the stop has already spoken. A planned loss, then the top works.

wrong.A shakeout; buy it back now: Buy again only on a new trigger over the level, never under the neckline.
wrong.Hold; the neckline is support: The stop is the exit. It was hit at 143.35; there is nothing to hold.

questions.q: The trigger day prints 1.0x its average volume. Does the trade still count?
choices: Yes; volume is a cue, no gate
No; it needs 2x the average
No; wait for more volume first
Yes; volume is ignored in grading
questions.answer: Yes; volume is a cue, no gate
questions.why: Yes. The card has no hard volume rule. Trigger-day volume at 1.25x or more of the 50-day average is a grading plus, so light volume does not cancel the trade. It only forgoes the plus. ICLR triggered on 1.0x its average volume, took three weeks to reach 3R, and then ran 25%. Bulkowski finds the same lean for rounding tops: heavy breakout volume suggests better performance.
questions.lesson_line: Volume grades the trigger. It does not decide it.

wrong.No; it needs 2x the average: There is no volume gate on this card. Heavy volume grades the day up; light volume does not cancel it.
wrong.No; wait for more volume first: The trigger is the trade over the level, not the volume. Waiting is a missed entry.
wrong.Yes; volume is ignored in grading: Volume does count as a cue. Trigger-day volume at 1.25x or more of the 50-day average is a grading plus.

questions.simple: Yes, because volume only adds to the grade and does not decide the trade.

reasons: the volume cue is a proposed card criterion

questions.story: The index sits under its 50-day in a correction, and the reading is Yellow. A leader's three-peak top broke its neckline, the fall stayed shallow, and now it trades over the right-shoulder high.
questions.q: How does the setting grade?
choices: A grading plus; the best setting
Pass; a correction means no longs
Lower grade; the market is weak
Neutral; the market is no factor
questions.answer: A grading plus; the best setting
questions.why: A grading plus. The card says best when the market itself is correcting and the stock refuses to break down. In our run, SPY under its 50-day gave +0.30R against a +0.12R baseline. The reading still applies: Yellow means smaller and fewer, and in Orange only A+ setups.
questions.lesson_line: A leader that holds up while the market falls is the one to own when the market turns.

wrong.Pass; a correction means no longs: A correction is not a ban. Yellow allows a buy, smaller and fewer. Red is the reading that is mostly cash.
wrong.Lower grade; the market is weak: A weak market with a leader that holds up is the cue, not a mark against it.
wrong.Neutral; the market is no factor: The card names a correcting market, with the stock refusing to break down, as the best setting.

questions.simple: A leader that holds up while the market falls is the best setting for this setup.

deeper.example: MUSA, early 2022: a 7% break under the neckline during the correction, recovered in three weeks. The trigger at 184.97 was followed by a 40% run, 39.0R at best.

reasons: a number from our own run that can change
rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)

questions.q: The last third trails the 10-day for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one, out on the first touch.
questions.why: False. The rule is a close below the line, not a touch. Our rulebook trails the 10-day average for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones, and says to sell on a close below it. A dip that touches the line and closes back above it does not sell the position. ICLR took three weeks to reach 3R and then ran 25%, which is the case for letting the trail decide the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.
questions.simple: False, because you sell on a close below the average, not on a touch during the day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule E52

questions.q: Bought at 22.71 with the stop at 22.30. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 23.94. One R is the fill minus the stop, so 3R is the fill plus three times that gap. The hard rule is to sell a third at 3R. MGM's trade reached 3R in 5 days.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R once you are filled. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill plus three times the gap down to the stop, which comes to 23.94.

reasons: a computed key

questions.story: Your failed-top long is up 2R. The head sits a little above here. A friend says the head is the target, sell it all there.
questions.q: What is the head on our card?
choices: A level to watch for sellers
The exit for the whole position
A ceiling the stock cannot pass
The place to add to the position
questions.answer: A level to watch for sellers
questions.why: A reference level, not a rule. Our card calls the head the first place sellers may return. Brandt's target is the right-shoulder high plus the distance from the head down to the post-break low, which is not the head itself. Our exits are the trims at 3R and 5R and then the trail, and the head does not replace them. In our run 75% of version-B triggers later traded over the head within 60 bars.
questions.lesson_line: The head is where to expect sellers, not where to sell everything.

wrong.The exit for the whole position: Our exits are thirds at 3R and 5R and a trail on the average, not one price.
wrong.A ceiling the stock cannot pass: In our run 75% of version-B triggers later traded over the head within 60 bars.
wrong.The place to add to the position: The head is a reference, not a buy level. Our buy is the first trade over the right-shoulder high.

questions.simple: The head is a place to watch for sellers, not a price to sell everything.

reasons: the head as a reference is a proposed card line

questions.q: A failed top triggers in a stock that has already run up for over a year. How do we grade it?
choices: Lower; it is late in the advance
A+; the failure is the signal
No change; age does not matter
Higher; a long run shows strength
questions.answer: Lower; it is late in the advance
questions.why: Lower. Our card grades a failed top lower when the stock has already run for a year or more, because a failed top late in a long advance can be the last push. Edwards and Magee: a formation that does not work is a warning that a genuine turn is near. GOOGL in 2026 triggered at 351.60, stalled under the 50-day and the neckline, reached 0.8R, and the stock fell 20% by late October. Lower is a grade, not a ban.
questions.lesson_line: A failed top a year into a run can be the last push. Grade it down.

wrong.A+; the failure is the signal: The failure counts; the age of the advance counts against it. Late in a long advance, it grades lower.
wrong.No change; age does not matter: Age does matter on our card: a failed top late in a long advance grades lower. GOOGL in 2026 stalled under its 50-day and fell 20% after its trigger.
wrong.Higher; a long run shows strength: Strength is why the stock ran, not proof this top will hold. Edwards and Magee warn that a failed top is a sign a genuine turn is near.

questions.simple: Lower, because a failed top late in a long run can turn out to be the last push up.

deeper.counter: The shape can be clean and the timing still late. A failed top a year into a run grades lower because it can be the last push, not because the pattern is bad. GOOGL in 2026 triggered at 351.60, stalled under the 50-day and the neckline, reached only 0.8R, then fell 20% by late October.

reasons: the late-stage cue is a proposed card criterion

questions.story: A three-peak top broke its neckline. The lowest close sat 10.9% under it. Then the stock came all the way back and trades over the right-shoulder high.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: No; the top had already worked
Yes; version B, a break bought back
Yes; the head is the profit target
No; any close below it ends the setup
questions.answer: No; the top had already worked
questions.why: No. A fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked, and this one closed 10.9% under it. That is a completed top and a full V recovery, not a failed break. CSCO's buy over 62.04 in this case was stopped at 0R. Version B needs a break that stays shallow before it is bought back, and Bulkowski's busted tops drop no more than 10% before they turn.
questions.lesson_line: A failed break stays shallow. A deep break that climbs back is a different chart.

wrong.Yes; version B, a break bought back: Version B is a shallow break bought back. This fall went past the 10% line, so the top worked.
wrong.Yes; the head is the profit target: No setup, no target. The head is a reference on a valid trade only.
wrong.No; any close below it ends the setup: Version B needs at least one close under the neckline. A close under it does not end the setup; a fall past 10% does.

questions.simple: No, because a fall of more than 10% under the neckline means the top worked and the setup is gone.

deeper.example: CSCO closed 10.9% under its neckline before it climbed all the way back. The shape looked like a failed break, and the rule said otherwise: more than 10% and the top worked. The buy over 62.04 was stopped at 0R. The line is sharp on purpose, and 10.9% is past it.

reasons: the deep-break line is a proposed card rule
rests on one near-miss from our own bars

questions.story: The trigger fills at 100.00. The trigger day's low is 95.80, so the honest stop sits about 4.2% below.
questions.q: What now?
choices: Size it down to fit the risk
Pull the stop in to about 3%
Use the undercut low as the stop
Buy full size anyway, stop as is
questions.answer: Size it down to fit the risk
questions.why: Size it down to the risk, or skip. Stop first: the stop goes a few cents under the trigger day's low, and the size comes from the stop. Shares = account x risk % / (entry - stop), rounded down, so a wider stop means fewer shares. If the stop is more than about 3% under the entry, size it down to the risk or skip. Pulling the stop in to fit, or using the undercut low, are both mistakes.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, then size from the stop. If it does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

wrong.Pull the stop in to about 3%: The rulebook sets the stop first and the size from it. A stop pulled in to fit the size is the honest stop moved, not the risk solved.
wrong.Use the undercut low as the stop: The undercut low is the invalidation line, not the stop. It is usually far more than 3% away.
wrong.Buy full size anyway, stop as is: The size comes from the stop. A wider stop with the same share count risks more than the plan allows.

questions.simple: Size the trade down to fit the risk, or skip it, since you never move the stop to fit the size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rules A3 and A5
the 4.2% is a computed figure in the story

questions.q: A brief, shallow undercut under 6% is the A+ form of the failure; 6% to 10% grades lower.
questions.why: True. On our card a brief, shallow undercut under 6% below the neckline is the A+ form, and 6% to 10% grades lower. Past 10% the setup is gone. In our run undercuts under 3% came to +0.12R, 3% to 6% came to +0.15R, and 6% to 10% came to +0.05R, where the interval crosses zero. It is a lean, not a gate.
questions.lesson_line: Under 6% is the A+ form of the failed break. From 6% to 10% it grades lower.
questions.simple: True, because a shallow undercut under 6% is the best form, and one from 6% to 10% grades lower.

reasons: the undercut-depth cue is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: The stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day on average. The most you may own?
choices: 30,000 shares, 1% of daily volume
300,000 shares, a tenth of the day
150,000 shares, 5% of daily volume
No ceiling with a tight stop
questions.why: 30,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000. Our card says the same: the position is at most 1% of average daily volume. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.300,000 shares, a tenth of the day: That is a tenth of the day's volume, far past the 1% ceiling.
wrong.No ceiling with a tight stop: The ceiling has no exception for a tight stop. The rule is 1% of average daily volume.
wrong.150,000 shares, 5% of daily volume: That is 5% of the day's volume, well past the 1% ceiling.

questions.simple: One percent of 3,000,000 is 30,000, and we never own more than that.

reasons: a computed key

questions.story: A clean failed top on a $12 stock that trades about $6 million a day.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: No; its volume is under the limit
No; the stock price is too low
Yes; a clean pattern is still clean
Yes, but only in a small position
questions.answer: No; its volume is under the limit
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. At $12 the price passes, but about $6 million a day fails the volume test. The pattern can be clean and the stock is still not ours. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: A clean pattern in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes; a clean pattern is still clean: The pattern may be clean, but illiquid stocks are not even watched.
wrong.Yes, but only in a small position: The rule screens the stock, not the size. A small position in a stock under the minimums still breaks it.
wrong.No; the stock price is too low: $12 clears the $10 minimum. The failure is the volume: about $6 million a day is under $20 million.

questions.simple: No, because the stock trades far less than $20 million a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule B23

questions.story: Your failed-top long closed at 2.7R. The next morning it opens at 3.3R.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Sell a third right at the open
Wait for the close to decide
Sell all of it at the open
Hold it all; let it keep running
questions.answer: Sell a third right at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. Yesterday's close of 2.7R was under 3R, but the open at 3.3R is past it, so the 3R third comes off right there. Another third waits at 5R and the last third trails, and the stop goes to breakeven at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for the close to decide: The rule is to take the trim at the open once the day opens above the level, not to wait for the close.
wrong.Sell all of it at the open: Only a third comes off at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Hold it all; let it keep running: The rest does keep running. The rule still takes the first third at the open.

questions.simple: Take the third off at the open, because the open is already past the 3R level.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule F63

questions.story: A stock rolled over in a slow curve for eight weeks, dipped under the curve's lowest low, and recovered. Now it trades over the curve's high.
questions.q: Which is it, and where is the trigger?
choices: Failed rounded top; the dome high
A flat base; the top of the box
Mean reversion; the flush day
Failed H&S; the right-shoulder high
questions.answer: Failed rounded top; the dome high
questions.why: A failed rounded top. The dome first broke its lower rim, the lowest low of the arc, then recovered. By our current default, the buy comes as price trades over the dome high. A slow curve is not a box, so it is not a flat base.
questions.lesson_line: A box that breaks up is a flat base. A dome that lost its rim and came back is ours.

wrong.A flat base; the top of the box: A flat base holds one range 15% deep or less with a flat top tapped twice. A curve that dipped under its lowest low and recovered is not a box.
wrong.Failed H&S; the right-shoulder high: The story has no three peaks and no shoulders, only a slow curve. A failed head-and-shoulders has three peaks over a neckline.
wrong.Mean reversion; the flush day: A mean-reversion long buys the turn on the flush day itself and is out in 1 to 5 sessions. This curve took eight weeks, and the buy comes over its high.

questions.simple: A dome that lost its lower rim and then recovered is a failed rounded top, not a box.

Stop under the undercut low instead

No; but never re-enter this stock

questions.story: A stock dropped 8% in one day into its 50-day, above every prior swing low, and bounced that afternoon. A trader buys the bounce and plans to sell at the 20-day within a few sessions.

A failed head-and-shoulders
A flat base breakout
A 2B, a broken low bought back
questions.why: Mean reversion. A mean-reversion long buys the turn on the flush day itself, into a level. It is out in 1 to 5 sessions at the average. A failed H&S waits weeks for the undercut to be bought back. Then it waits for the trade over the right-shoulder high, and holds for a trend. wrong.A 2B, a broken low bought back: A 2B breaks one prior swing low and is bought when price reclaims it. No prior low broke here, so there is nothing to reclaim.
wrong.A flat base breakout: A flat base holds one range 15% deep or less with a flat top tapped twice and breaks out over it. One 8% drop and a bounce is no box.

questions.simple: This buys a flush day and sells within days at the average, which is mean reversion, not a failed top.

deeper.example: ICLR triggered on 1.0x volume, took three weeks to reach 3R, then ran 25%. A mean-reversion trade is gone in 1 to 5 sessions. A failed top waits for a trend.

The 10-day only
The neckline only

questions.story: The neckline broke four days ago on heavy volume. The stock still sits above its 200-day. Today price bounces back up to the neckline from below. The right-shoulder high is 6% higher.
questions.q: Buy now?
choices: No; that is the return move
Yes; the break is being bought back
